Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: First-time unilateral headache with classic migraine features (visual aura, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, family history, no neurological deficit).  
Most consistent diagnosis: Migraine with aura.  
Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript & DDx):  
• Subarachnoid hemorrhage – needs exclusion because of sudden onset and vomiting, though pain only 6/10 and no neuro signs.  
• Carotid/vertebral artery dissection – less likely; no neck pain/trauma or focal deficits.  

Working diagnosis: Migraine with aura (first presentation).  
Plan: Trial symptomatic therapy; arrange same-day in-person review for full neurological examination; advise emergency care if worsening, severe escalation, new neuro deficits, or lack of response to medication.

- Recommend ibuprofen (dose not documented) plus an anti-emetic (pharmacy supply) and oral sugary carbonated drink for acute migraine relief.  
- Arrange face-to-face appointment later today for full neurological and fundoscopic examination; patient to cancel if symptoms fully resolve.  
- Safety-net advice provided: attend ED if sudden worsening, peak severity, confusion, weakness, or visual loss.  
- Education on migraine nature, typical duration (4–72 h), and treatment ladder discussed.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Migraine with aura – High likelihood: fits unilateral pain, visual aura, N/V, photophobia, family history, absence of neuro deficit.  
2. Subarachnoid hemorrhage – Moderate likelihood: abrupt “first” headache with vomiting; needs exclusion despite lower pain rating and lack of neuro signs.  
3. Carotid/vertebral artery dissection – Low–Moderate likelihood: unilateral headache with visual disturbance and dizziness; absence of neck pain or focal signs lowers probability.
